claim: Candida albicans is both a member of the healthy human microbiome and a major pathogen in immunocompromised individuals.
source: Candida albicans is both a member of the healthy human microbiome and a major pathogen in immunocompromised individuals.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about C. albicans' dual role.

claim: C. albicans infections are typically treated with azole inhibitors of ergosterol biosynthesis.
source: Infections are typically treated with azole inhibitors of ergosterol biosynthesis often leading to drug resistance.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge about treatment approaches.

claim: Azole treatment often leads to drug resistance in C. albicans.
source: Infections are typically treated with azole inhibitors of ergosterol biosynthesis often leading to drug resistance.
evidence: This is supported by established clinical observations and literature.

claim: The study analyzed 43 isolates from 11 oral candidiasis patients.
source: Here, we leveraged next-generation sequencing to analyze 43 isolates from 11 oral candidiasis patients.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by Table 1.

claim: LOH events were commonly associated with acquired resistance.
source: LOH events were commonly associated with acquired resistance, and SNPs in 240 genes may be related to host adaptation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: SNPs in 240 genes may be related to host adaptation.
source: LOH events were commonly associated with acquired resistance, and SNPs in 240 genes may be related to host adaptation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Most aneuploidies were transient and did not correlate with drug resistance.
source: Conversely, most aneuploidies were transient and did not correlate with drug resistance.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Isolates varied in adherence, filamentation, and virulence.
source: Our analysis also shows that isolates also varied in adherence, filamentation, and virulence.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: Virtually all humans are colonized with Candida albicans.
source: Virtually all humans are colonized with Candida albicans, but in some individuals this benign commensal organism becomes a serious, life-threatening pathogen.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about C. albicans colonization.

claim: C. albicans possesses phenotypic switching as a trait that promotes pathogenicity.
source: C. albicans possesses an arsenal of traits that promote its pathogenicity, including phenotypic switching (Alby and Bennett, 2009), yeast–hyphae transition (Kumamoto and Vinces, 2005) and the secretion of molecules that promote adhesion to abiotic surfaces (Chandra et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alby and Bennett, 2009.

claim: C. albicans possesses yeast-hyphae transition as a trait that promotes pathogenicity.
source: C. albicans possesses an arsenal of traits that promote its pathogenicity, including phenotypic switching (Alby and Bennett, 2009), yeast–hyphae transition (Kumamoto and Vinces, 2005) and the secretion of molecules that promote adhesion to abiotic surfaces (Chandra et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumamoto and Vinces, 2005.

claim: C. albicans secretes molecules that promote adhesion to abiotic surfaces.
source: C. albicans possesses an arsenal of traits that promote its pathogenicity, including phenotypic switching (Alby and Bennett, 2009), yeast–hyphae transition (Kumamoto and Vinces, 2005) and the secretion of molecules that promote adhesion to abiotic surfaces (Chandra et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chandra et al., 2001.

claim: Systemic C. albicans infections are fatal in 42% of cases despite antifungal therapies.
source: systemic C. albicans infections are fatal in 42% of cases (Wisplinghoff et al., 2003), despite the use of antifungal therapies, and C. albicans is the fourth most common infection in hospitals (Gudlaugsson et al., 2003; Pappas et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wisplinghoff et al., 2003.

claim: C. albicans is the fourth most common infection in hospitals.
source: systemic C. albicans infections are fatal in 42% of cases (Wisplinghoff et al., 2003), despite the use of antifungal therapies, and C. albicans is the fourth most common infection in hospitals (Gudlaugsson et al., 2003; Pappas et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gudlaugsson et al., 2003 and Pappas et al., 2003.

claim: Polyenes (e.g., Amphotericin B) are used sparingly due to toxicity.
source: Polyenes (e.g., Amphotericin B) are used sparingly due to toxicity (Rex et al., 1994), whereas azoles (e.g., fluconazole) are used widely because they can be administered orally and have few side effects (Rex et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rex et al., 1994.

claim: Azoles (e.g., fluconazole) are used widely because they can be administered orally and have few side effects.
source: Polyenes (e.g., Amphotericin B) are used sparingly due to toxicity (Rex et al., 1994), whereas azoles (e.g., fluconazole) are used widely because they can be administered orally and have few side effects (Rex et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rex et al., 2003.

claim: Azoles are fungistatic (inhibit growth but do not kill).
source: However, resistance to the azoles arises within the commensal population of the treated individual, primarily because azoles are fungistatic (inhibit growth but do not kill) (Cowen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cowen et al., 2002.

claim: The intensity of fluconazole use is driving the appearance of resistant isolates.
source: Epidemiological data suggest that the intensity of fluconazole use is driving the appearance of resistant isolates (Pfaller et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pfaller et al., 1998.

claim: Drug resistance can increase during an infection through the acquisition of aneuploidies due to genomic plasticity and rapid evolutionary selection.
source: Studies of clinical isolates of C. albicans suggest that drug resistance can increase during an infection through the acquisition of aneuploidies (Selmecki et al., 2009) due to genomic plasticity and rapid evolutionary selection during infection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Selmecki et al., 2009.

claim: Increased activity or level of ERG11 reduces direct impact of fluconazole on its target.
source: First, increased activity or level of the enzymes of the ergosterol pathway (e.g., ERG11) reduces direct impact of the drug on its target (Asai et al., 1999; Oliver et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asai et al., 1999 and Oliver et al., 2007.

claim: Increased efflux of the drug from cells by ABC transporters (encoded by CDR1 and CDR2) reduces the effective intracellular drug concentration.
source: Second, increased efflux of the drug from cells by ABC transporters (encoded by CDR1 and CDR2) (Coste et al., 2006) or by the major facilitator superfamily efflux pump (encoded by MDR1) (Dunkel et al., 2008) reduces the effective intracellular drug concentration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coste et al., 2006.

claim: Increased efflux of the drug from cells by the major facilitator superfamily efflux pump (encoded by MDR1) reduces the effective intracellular drug concentration.
source: Second, increased efflux of the drug from cells by ABC transporters (encoded by CDR1 and CDR2) (Coste et al., 2006) or by the major facilitator superfamily efflux pump (encoded by MDR1) (Dunkel et al., 2008) reduces the effective intracellular drug concentration.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dunkel et al., 2008.

claim: Point mutations in genes encoding drug resistance proteins can result in azole resistance.
source: In both cases, such alterations can result from point mutations in genes encoding these proteins (Marichal et al., 1999), in transcription factors that regulate mRNA expression levels (MacPherson et al., 2005; Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008), or from increased copy number of the relevant genes, via genome rearrangements such as whole chromosome and segmental aneuploidies (Selmecki et al., 2006; 2008; 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marichal et al., 1999.

claim: Point mutations in transcription factors that regulate mRNA expression levels can result in azole resistance.
source: In both cases, such alterations can result from point mutations in genes encoding these proteins (Marichal et al., 1999), in transcription factors that regulate mRNA expression levels (MacPherson et al., 2005; Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008), or from increased copy number of the relevant genes, via genome rearrangements such as whole chromosome and segmental aneuploidies (Selmecki et al., 2006; 2008; 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacPherson et al., 2005; Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008.

claim: Increased copy number of relevant genes via genome rearrangements such as whole chromosome and segmental aneuploidies can result in azole resistance.
source: In both cases, such alterations can result from point mutations in genes encoding these proteins (Marichal et al., 1999), in transcription factors that regulate mRNA expression levels (MacPherson et al., 2005; Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008), or from increased copy number of the relevant genes, via genome rearrangements such as whole chromosome and segmental aneuploidies (Selmecki et al., 2006; 2008; 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Selmecki et al., 2006; 2008; 2009.

claim: Drug-resistant strains isolated following clinical treatment often exhibit loss of heterozygosity (LOH).
source: Indeed, the genomes of drug-resistant strains isolated following clinical treatment often exhibit large-scale changes, such as loss of heterozygosity (LOH) (Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel and Morschhauser, 2011), copy-number variation (CNV), including short segmental CNV, and whole chromosome aneuploidy (Selmecki et al., 2010) accompanied by point mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coste et al., 2006 and Dunkel and Morschhauser, 2011.

claim: Drug-resistant strains isolated following clinical treatment often exhibit copy-number variation (CNV), including short segmental CNV, and whole chromosome aneuploidy.
source: Indeed, the genomes of drug-resistant strains isolated following clinical treatment often exhibit large-scale changes, such as loss of heterozygosity (LOH) (Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel and Morschhauser, 2011), copy-number variation (CNV), including short segmental CNV, and whole chromosome aneuploidy (Selmecki et al., 2010) accompanied by point mutations.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Selmecki et al., 2010.

claim: C. albicans has conserved the genomic elements needed for mating.
source: Although C. albicans has conserved the genomic elements needed for mating, mating occurs instead through rare mating-competent haploids (Hickman et al., 2013) or via a parasexual cycle consisting of mating of diploid strains to form tetraploids followed by chromosome loss to regenerate diploids (Bennett and Johnson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hickman et al., 2013.

claim: C. albicans mating occurs through rare mating-competent haploids.
source: Although C. albicans has conserved the genomic elements needed for mating, mating occurs instead through rare mating-competent haploids (Hickman et al., 2013) or via a parasexual cycle consisting of mating of diploid strains to form tetraploids followed by chromosome loss to regenerate diploids (Bennett and Johnson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hickman et al., 2013.

claim: C. albicans mating occurs via a parasexual cycle consisting of mating of diploid strains to form tetraploids followed by chromosome loss to regenerate diploids.
source: Although C. albicans has conserved the genomic elements needed for mating, mating occurs instead through rare mating-competent haploids (Hickman et al., 2013) or via a parasexual cycle consisting of mating of diploid strains to form tetraploids followed by chromosome loss to regenerate diploids (Bennett and Johnson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bennett and Johnson, 2005.

claim: Previous studies in evolved isolates have focused on large-scale aberrations such as aneuploidies and LOH.
source: Studies in evolved isolates have implicated multiple mechanisms in drug resistance, but have focused on large-scale aberrations such as aneuploidies and LOH (Selmecki et al., 2008; 2009) or candidate genes (Perea et al., 2001; White et al., 2002), and do not comprehensively chart the genetic basis of adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Selmecki et al., 2008; 2009.

claim: Previous studies in evolved isolates have focused on candidate genes.
source: Studies in evolved isolates have implicated multiple mechanisms in drug resistance, but have focused on large-scale aberrations such as aneuploidies and LOH (Selmecki et al., 2008; 2009) or candidate genes (Perea et al., 2001; White et al., 2002), and do not comprehensively chart the genetic basis of adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Perea et al., 2001 and White et al., 2002.

claim: The isolates were obtained from HIV-infected patients with oropharyngeal candidiasis.
source: To study the in vivo evolution of azole resistance in C. albicans, we analyzed 43 longitudinal isolates from 11 HIV-infected patients with oropharyngeal candidiasis (White, 1997a; Perea et al., 2001) (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White, 1997a and Perea et al., 2001, and by Table 1.

claim: The isolates form a time series from each patient (2–16 isolates per series).
source: The isolates were previously collected during incidences of infection and form a time series from each patient (2–16 isolates per series; Figure 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Table 1 and Figures 1 and 2A.

claim: Each isolate was derived from a single colony and represents a single diploid genotype sampled from the within-host C. albicans population at the respective time point.
source: Each isolate was derived from a single colony, and thus, represents a single diploid genotype sampled from the within-host C. albicans population at the respective time point.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the sampling approach.

claim: The first isolate ('progenitor') was collected prior to any treatment with azole antifungals.
source: In each series, the first isolate ('progenitor') was collected prior to any treatment with azole antifungals and the remaining isolates were collected at later, typically consecutive, time points, culminating in the final 'endpoint' isolate (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data in Table 1.

claim: The progenitor isolates were more sensitive to fluconazole than subsequent isolates, as defined by the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC).
source: The progenitor isolates were more sensitive to fluconazole than subsequent isolates, as defined by the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) (Table 1, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by the MIC data in Table 1.

claim: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified segmental aneuploidy as a genomic alteration that may contribute to azole resistance.
source: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified several genomic alterations that may contribute to azole resistance, including segmental aneuploidy (Selmecki et al., 2006), and LOH across large chromosomal segments (Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008), as well as targeted alterations including increased expression of drug efflux genes (Coste et al., 2006), mutations in ergosterol biosynthetic genes (Asai et al., 1999; Oliver et al., 2007), and buffering by the chaperone heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Selmecki et al., 2006.

claim: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified LOH across large chromosomal segments as a genomic alteration that may contribute to azole resistance.
source: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified several genomic alterations that may contribute to azole resistance, including segmental aneuploidy (Selmecki et al., 2006), and LOH across large chromosomal segments (Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008), as well as targeted alterations including increased expression of drug efflux genes (Coste et al., 2006), mutations in ergosterol biosynthetic genes (Asai et al., 1999; Oliver et al., 2007), and buffering by the chaperone heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coste et al., 2006 and Dunkel et al., 2008.

claim: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified increased expression of drug efflux genes as a targeted alteration that may contribute to azole resistance.
source: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified several genomic alterations that may contribute to azole resistance, including segmental aneuploidy (Selmecki et al., 2006), and LOH across large chromosomal segments (Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008), as well as targeted alterations including increased expression of drug efflux genes (Coste et al., 2006), mutations in ergosterol biosynthetic genes (Asai et al., 1999; Oliver et al., 2007), and buffering by the chaperone heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coste et al., 2006.

claim: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified mutations in ergosterol biosynthetic genes as a targeted alteration that may contribute to azole resistance.
source: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified several genomic alterations that may contribute to azole resistance, including segmental aneuploidy (Selmecki et al., 2006), and LOH across large chromosomal segments (Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008), as well as targeted alterations including increased expression of drug efflux genes (Coste et al., 2006), mutations in ergosterol biosynthetic genes (Asai et al., 1999; Oliver et al., 2007), and buffering by the chaperone heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Asai et al., 1999 and Oliver et al., 2007.

claim: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified buffering by the chaperone heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) as a mechanism that may contribute to azole resistance.
source: Previous studies with some of these patient isolates identified several genomic alterations that may contribute to azole resistance, including segmental aneuploidy (Selmecki et al., 2006), and LOH across large chromosomal segments (Coste et al., 2006; Dunkel et al., 2008), as well as targeted alterations including increased expression of drug efflux genes (Coste et al., 2006), mutations in ergosterol biosynthetic genes (Asai et al., 1999; Oliver et al., 2007), and buffering by the chaperone heat shock protein 90 (Hsp90) (Cowen and Lindquist, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cowen and Lindquist, 2005.

claim: The genomic DNA of the isolates was sequenced using Illumina sequencing with 53-283X coverage, 103X on average.
source: We sequenced the genomic DNA of the isolates as well as the C. albicans lab strain, SC5314, using Illumina sequencing (53-283X coverage, 103X on average, 'Materials and methods', Table 1)
evidence: This is supported by the data in Table 1.

claim: The study validated the pipeline for detection of point mutations using Sequenom iPlex genotyping.
source: We validated our pipeline for detection of point mutations using Sequenom iPLex genotyping (Storm et al., 2003) ('Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by citation to Storm et al., 2003 and validation data in Table 2.

claim: 1973 SNPs in 27 isolates from nine clinical series were interrogated for iPLex genotyping.
source: We interrogated 1973 SNPs in 27 isolates from nine clinical series and found that the iPlex base calls matched 1853 (93.9%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Table 2) of the calls from our computational analysis of the sequencing data.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The iPlex base calls matched 1853 (93.9%) of the calls from computational analysis of the sequencing data.
source: We interrogated 1973 SNPs in 27 isolates from nine clinical series and found that the iPlex base calls matched 1853 (93.9%, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Table 2) of the calls from our computational analysis of the sequencing data.
evidence: This is supported by the data in Table 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Isolates within most series were clonally related, suggesting a single (primary) infection source.
source: We designated as background those polymorphisms those that are common to all isolates in a series, including the first ('progenitor') isolate (Figure 1A, purple) and use them to determine that isolates within most series were clonally related, suggesting a single (primary) infection source (Figure 1B,C, Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Patient 64 contained one C. albicans isolate (4018) and one C. dubliniensis isolate (4380).
source: Patient 64 contained one C. albicans isolate (4018) and one C. dubliniensis isolate (4380); therefore, we have excluded this series from further analysis.
evidence: This is supported by alignment analysis described in the text.

claim: At least one non-clonal C. albicans isolate was detected in three of the remaining ten patient series (PT 9,16, 42).
source: Additionally, we detected at least one non-clonal C. albicans isolate in three of the remaining ten patient series (PT 9,16, 42; Figure 2B, red), indicating that at least ∼36% of the 11 patients sampled carried more than one unrelated Candida strain.
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: At least ∼36% of the 11 patients sampled carried more than one unrelated Candida strain.
source: Additionally, we detected at least one non-clonal C. albicans isolate in three of the remaining ten patient series (PT 9,16, 42; Figure 2B, red), indicating that at least ∼36% of the 11 patients sampled carried more than one unrelated Candida strain.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of non-clonal isolates in 3 of 11 patients.

claim: Despite clonal relationships, the distance between isolates indicated significant genetic diversity within each patient series.
source: Despite these clonal relationships, the distance between isolates indicated significant genetic diversity within each patient series (Figure 2B), typically with each isolate differing by several thousand SNPs from its 'progenitor' isolate (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 2B and SNP data in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Each isolate typically differed by several thousand SNPs from its 'progenitor' isolate.
source: Despite these clonal relationships, the distance between isolates indicated significant genetic diversity within each patient series (Figure 2B), typically with each isolate differing by several thousand SNPs from its 'progenitor' isolate (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by SNP data in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Different isolates collected on the same day from the same patient (patient 14 [2440 and 2501] and patient 16 [3107 and 3119]) differed by 9668 and 18,291 SNPs, respectively.
source: However, the role of pre-existing diversity is supported by the observation that different isolates collected on the same day from the same patient (patient 14 [2440 and 2501] and patient 16 [3107 and 3119]) differed by 9668 and 18,291 SNPs, respectively (Figure 2—source data 1) and had very different fluconazole MIC levels (Table 1) and different fitness phenotypes (see below), although in each case the strains were clearly genetically related (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by SNP data in Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Isolates collected on the same day from the same patient had very different fluconazole MIC levels.
source: However, the role of pre-existing diversity is supported by the observation that different isolates collected on the same day from the same patient (patient 14 [2440 and 2501] and patient 16 [3107 and 3119]) differed by 9668 and 18,291 SNPs, respectively (Figure 2—source data 1) and had very different fluconazole MIC levels (Table 1) and different fitness phenotypes (see below), although in each case the strains were clearly genetically related (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by MIC data in Table 1.

claim: A population of related but divergent genotypes of the same lineage exists within a given patient.
source: Thus, we conclude that a population of related but divergent genotypes of the same lineage exists within a given patient.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic diversity observed in isolates from the same patient.

claim: LOH events were detected in all of the series.
source: LOH events were detected in all of the series and were often persistent, recurrent, and associated with increased drug resistance (Figures 3 and 4, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: LOH events were often persistent, recurrent, and associated with increased drug resistance.
source: LOH events were detected in all of the series and were often persistent, recurrent, and associated with increased drug resistance (Figures 3 and 4, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Three of four LOH events in Patient 1 were persistent and associated with an increase in MIC.
source: For example, three of four LOH events in Patient 1 were persistent and associated with an increase in MIC and both of these events were recurrent, such that LOH events in these genomic regions coincided with increases in MIC in other patients.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Highly recurrent LOH events occurred on the right arm of chromosome 3 in Patients 1, 9, 14, 16, 42, and 59.
source: Highly recurrent LOH events occurred on the right arm of chromosome 3 (in Patients 1, 9, 14, 16, 42, and 59; Figure 3A, Figure 4A,B,D,F,H, Figure 3—source data 1) and on the left arm of chromosome 5 (in Patients 1, 14, 15, and 43; Figure 3A, Figure 4B,C,G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3A and 4A,B,D,F,H.

claim: Highly recurrent LOH events occurred on the left arm of chromosome 5 in Patients 1, 14, 15, and 43.
source: Highly recurrent LOH events occurred on the right arm of chromosome 3 (in Patients 1, 9, 14, 16, 42, and 59; Figure 3A, Figure 4A,B,D,F,H, Figure 3—source data 1) and on the left arm of chromosome 5 (in Patients 1, 14, 15, and 43; Figure 3A, Figure 4B,C,G, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3A and 4B,C,G.

claim: Chromosome 3 includes genes encoding the Cdr1 and Cdr2 efflux pumps and the Mrr1 transcription factor that regulates the Mdr1 major facilitator superfamily efflux pump.
source: These regions include key genes implicated in drug resistance: on Chromosome 3, genes encoding the Cdr1 and Cdr2 efflux pumps and the Mrr1 transcription factor that regulates the Mdr1 major facilitator superfamily efflux pump (Schubert et al., 2011), and on Chromosome 5, genes encoding the drug target Erg11, and Tac1, a transcription factor that positively regulates expression of CDR1 and CDR2 (Coste et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schubert et al., 2011.

claim: Chromosome 5 includes genes encoding the drug target Erg11, and Tac1, a transcription factor that positively regulates expression of CDR1 and CDR2.
source: These regions include key genes implicated in drug resistance: on Chromosome 3, genes encoding the Cdr1 and Cdr2 efflux pumps and the Mrr1 transcription factor that regulates the Mdr1 major facilitator superfamily efflux pump (Schubert et al., 2011), and on Chromosome 5, genes encoding the drug target Erg11, and Tac1, a transcription factor that positively regulates expression of CDR1 and CDR2 (Coste et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coste et al., 2006.

claim: The extent of persistence and recurrence of the Chr3R LOH is statistically significant (p < 5 × 10−4).
source: The extent of persistence and recurrence of these two LOH events is statistically significant under a naïve binary model (p < 5 × 10−4 for the Chr3R LOH; p < 0.01 for the Chr5L LOH).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the LOH data.

claim: The extent of persistence and recurrence of the Chr5L LOH is statistically significant (p < 0.01).
source: The extent of persistence and recurrence of these two LOH events is statistically significant under a naïve binary model (p < 5 × 10−4 for the Chr3R LOH; p < 0.01 for the Chr5L LOH).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the LOH data.

claim: The recurrence of LOH events that coincide with changes in MIC suggests that they have been positively selected to rise in frequency relative to the progenitor strain.
source: The recurrence of LOH events that coincide with changes in MIC suggests that they have been positively selected to rise in frequency relative to the progenitor strain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed correlation between LOH and MIC changes.

claim: Some of the recurrent LOH events may have been difficult to detect previously on SNP arrays due to the relative paucity of SNPs in those regions in the reference strain, SC5413.
source: Notably, some of the recurrent LOH events may have been difficult to detect previously on SNP arrays (Forche et al., 2008; Forche et al., 2004; Forche et al., 2005) due to the relative paucity of SNPs in those regions in the reference strain, SC5413, itself a clinical isolate.
evidence: This is an inference based on technical limitations of previous methods, supported by citations to Forche et al., 2008; 2004; 2005.

claim: There were 131 driver mutations in 86 ORFs from 18 LOH regions from the 10 clonal patient series.
source: There were 131 such mutations in 86 ORFs from 18 LOH regions from the 10 clonal patient series (Table 1 and Figure 5; Figure 5—source data 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—source data 1B,C.

claim: A nonsynonymous homozygous change in ERG11 was associated with the formation of the persistent LOH on the left arm of chromosome 5 in Patient 1.
source: For example, a nonsynonymous homozygous change in the fluconazole drug target ERG11 was associated with the formation of the persistent LOH on the left arm of chromosome 5 in Patient 1 (Figure 3A), consistent with previous reports (White, 1997b), as was TAC1 in Patient 42.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A and citation to White, 1997b.

claim: A nonsynonymous homozygous change in TAC1 was associated with the formation of the persistent LOH in Patient 42.
source: For example, a nonsynonymous homozygous change in the fluconazole drug target ERG11 was associated with the formation of the persistent LOH on the left arm of chromosome 5 in Patient 1 (Figure 3A), consistent with previous reports (White, 1997b), as was TAC1 in Patient 42.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis.

claim: The persistent and recurrent LOH on the right arm of chromosome 3 in Patients 9 and 16 was associated with the presence of a homozygous mutation in MRR1.
source: In another example, the persistent and recurrent LOH on the right arm of chromosome 3 in Patients 9 and 16 (Figure 4A,D) was associated with the presence of a homozygous mutation in MRR1 (Schubert et al., 2011), a regulator of MDR1 expression.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A,D and citation to Schubert et al., 2011.

claim: Mutations were found in genes involved in cell adhesion (ALS3,5 and 7 and HYR3).
source: Other mutations were in genes not previously related to fluconazole resistance, including cell adhesion (ALS3,5 and 7 and HYR3; [Hoyer et al., 1998; Sheppard et al., 2004; Hoyer et al., 2008]), filamentous growth (FGR14, FGR28, and EFH, [Uhl et al., 2003; Connolly et al., 2013]), and biofilm formation (BCR1 and YAK1; [Nobile and Mitchell, 2005; Goyard et al., 2008; Noble et al., 2010; Nobile et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hoyer et al., 1998; Sheppard et al., 2004; Hoyer et al., 2008.

claim: Mutations were found in genes involved in filamentous growth (FGR14, FGR28, and EFH).
source: Other mutations were in genes not previously related to fluconazole resistance, including cell adhesion (ALS3,5 and 7 and HYR3; [Hoyer et al., 1998; Sheppard et al., 2004; Hoyer et al., 2008]), filamentous growth (FGR14, FGR28, and EFH, [Uhl et al., 2003; Connolly et al., 2013]), and biofilm formation (BCR1 and YAK1; [Nobile and Mitchell, 2005; Goyard et al., 2008; Noble et al., 2010; Nobile et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Uhl et al., 2003 and Connolly et al., 2013.

claim: Mutations were found in genes involved in biofilm formation (BCR1 and YAK1).
source: Other mutations were in genes not previously related to fluconazole resistance, including cell adhesion (ALS3,5 and 7 and HYR3; [Hoyer et al., 1998; Sheppard et al., 2004; Hoyer et al., 2008]), filamentous growth (FGR14, FGR28, and EFH, [Uhl et al., 2003; Connolly et al., 2013]), and biofilm formation (BCR1 and YAK1; [Nobile and Mitchell, 2005; Goyard et al., 2008; Noble et al., 2010; Nobile et al., 2012]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nobile and Mitchell, 2005; Goyard et al., 2008; Noble et al., 2010; Nobile et al., 2012.

claim: Aneuploidies were evident in at least one isolate from 80% (8/10) of the clonal patient series.
source: Aneuploidies, either whole chromosomal or segmental, were evident in at least one isolate from 80% (8/10) of the clonal patient series, with the most prevalent aneuploidies involving Chromosome 5 (6 of 8 patients with at least one aneuploid isolate; Figure 3A and Figure 4B–G, green).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3A and 4B-G.

claim: The most prevalent aneuploidies involved Chromosome 5 (6 of 8 patients with at least one aneuploid isolate).
source: Aneuploidies, either whole chromosomal or segmental, were evident in at least one isolate from 80% (8/10) of the clonal patient series, with the most prevalent aneuploidies involving Chromosome 5 (6 of 8 patients with at least one aneuploid isolate; Figure 3A and Figure 4B–G, green).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3A and 4B-G.

claim: Persistent aneuploidies were rarer and were not consistently associated with adaptive increases in MIC levels.
source: In contrast to the persistence of most LOH events, persistent aneuploidies were rarer and were not consistently associated with adaptive increases in MIC levels (Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In 4 of the 6 patients with a Chromosome 5 LOH, the isolate with an LOH event also harbors a Chromosome 5 trisomy or is preceded by an isolate with a Chromosome 5 trisomy.
source: For example, in 4 of the 6 patients with a Chromosome 5 LOH, the isolate with an LOH event also harbors a Chromosome 5 trisomy or is preceded by an isolate with a Chromosome 5 trisomy.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Aneuploidy could contribute to the evolution of LOH by increasing the likelihood of its occurrence.
source: While we cannot definitively infer an ordering of events from our singly sampled isolates, we hypothesize that aneuploidy could contribute to the evolution of LOH by increasing the likelihood of its occurrence.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the observed association between aneuploidy and LOH.

claim: Persistent nonsynonymous coding SNPs were identified within 1470 genes outside LOH tracts.
source: We identified persistent nonsynonymous coding SNPs within 1470 genes outside LOH tracts, 167 of them harboring 336 driver-like polymorphisms (Figure 5—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—source data 1B.

claim: 167 genes harbored 336 driver-like polymorphisms.
source: We identified persistent nonsynonymous coding SNPs within 1470 genes outside LOH tracts, 167 of them harboring 336 driver-like polymorphisms (Figure 5—source data 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—source data 1B.

claim: 240 polymorphic genes were identified that are more likely to have contributed to adaptation.
source: Applying the recurrence filter (i.e., persistent nonsynonymous SNPs that appeared in the same ORFs in three or more patient series), we identified 240 polymorphic genes that are more likely to have contributed to adaptation (Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—source data 1A.

claim: The number of 240 recurrent genes is higher than expected by chance (empirical p < 10−4).
source: This number of genes is higher than expected by chance (empirical p < 10−4 based on a Poisson model of background mutation, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis using a Poisson model.

claim: The coding sequence for the 240 recurrent genes is longer than average (2.21 ± 1.53 kb vs 1.83 ± 1.29 kb for non-recurrent persistent genes, p < 3.68 × 10−5).
source: Though the coding sequence for these 240 recurrent genes is longer than average (2.21 ± 1.53 kb vs 1.83 ± 1.29 kb for non-recurrent persistent genes, p < 3.68 × 10−5, t-test), and thus a larger target for mutation, our simulation accounts for gene length.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis using a t-test.

claim: 17 persistent recurrently polymorphic genes also had driver-like polymorphisms.
source: Notably, 17 persistent recurrently polymorphic genes also had driver-like polymorphisms, eight of which were also homozygosed in an LOH tract in at least one patient series (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—source data 1A,B,C.

claim: Eight of the 17 persistent recurrently polymorphic genes with driver-like polymorphisms were also homozygosed in an LOH tract in at least one patient series.
source: Notably, 17 persistent recurrently polymorphic genes also had driver-like polymorphisms, eight of which were also homozygosed in an LOH tract in at least one patient series (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—source data 1A,B,C.

claim: Polymorphisms in 166 of the 240 genes appeared together with an increase in MIC.
source: Finally, polymorphisms in 166 of the 240 genes appeared together with an increase in MIC and are thus stronger candidates for making a significant functional contribution to resistance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1D, empirical p < 10−5 based a binomial model, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1D.

claim: The association of polymorphisms in 166 genes with MIC increase is statistically significant (empirical p < 10−5).
source: Finally, polymorphisms in 166 of the 240 genes appeared together with an increase in MIC and are thus stronger candidates for making a significant functional contribution to resistance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—source data 1D, empirical p < 10−5 based a binomial model, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis using a binomial model.

claim: The set of 240 recurrently mutated genes was enriched for fungal-type cell wall genes (18 genes, p < 0.0012).
source: The set of 240 recurrently mutated genes was enriched for fungal-type cell wall (18 genes, p < 0.0012) and cell surface genes (24 genes, p < 0.00012), including several members in each of three cell wall gene families important for biofilm formation and virulence (Hoyer et al., 2008): the Hyr/Iff proteins (HYR1 and 3, IFF8 and 6), the ALS adhesins (ALS1-4,7,9), and the PGA-30-like proteins (seven genes) (Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: The set of 240 recurrently mutated genes was enriched for cell surface genes (24 genes, p < 0.00012).
source: The set of 240 recurrently mutated genes was enriched for fungal-type cell wall (18 genes, p < 0.0012) and cell surface genes (24 genes, p < 0.00012), including several members in each of three cell wall gene families important for biofilm formation and virulence (Hoyer et al., 2008): the Hyr/Iff proteins (HYR1 and 3, IFF8 and 6), the ALS adhesins (ALS1-4,7,9), and the PGA-30-like proteins (seven genes) (Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: The Hyr/Iff proteins, ALS adhesins, and PGA-30-like proteins are cell wall gene families important for biofilm formation and virulence.
source: The set of 240 recurrently mutated genes was enriched for fungal-type cell wall (18 genes, p < 0.0012) and cell surface genes (24 genes, p < 0.00012), including several members in each of three cell wall gene families important for biofilm formation and virulence (Hoyer et al., 2008): the Hyr/Iff proteins (HYR1 and 3, IFF8 and 6), the ALS adhesins (ALS1-4,7,9), and the PGA-30-like proteins (seven genes) (Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hoyer et al., 2008.

claim: All three cell wall gene families (Hyr/Iff, ALS, PGA-30-like) are specifically expanded in the genomes of pathogenic Candida species.
source: All three families are specifically expanded in the genomes of pathogenic Candida species (Butler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Butler et al., 2009.

claim: Seven members of the FGR genes, involved in filamentous growth and specifically expanded in C. albicans, are among the 240 genes.
source: In addition, seven members of the FGR genes (Uhl et al., 2003), involved in filamentous growth and specifically expanded in C. albicans (Butler et al., 2009), are also among the 240 genes (Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Uhl et al., 2003 and Butler et al., 2009.

claim: AXL1 was the most recurrently mutated gene outside of an LOH region, persistently mutated in eight series.
source: The most recurrently mutated gene outside of an LOH region was AXL1 that encodes a putative endoprotease, whose transcript is upregulated in an RHE model of oral candidiasis and in clinical isolates from HIV+ patients with oral candidiasis (Zakikhany et al., 2007). The gene is persistently mutated in eight series, (three of which were driver mutations), followed by ten genes mutated in seven series (Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—source data 1A and citation to Zakikhany et al., 2007.

claim: AXL1 encodes a putative endoprotease whose transcript is upregulated in an RHE model of oral candidiasis and in clinical isolates from HIV+ patients with oral candidiasis.
source: The most recurrently mutated gene outside of an LOH region was AXL1 that encodes a putative endoprotease, whose transcript is upregulated in an RHE model of oral candidiasis and in clinical isolates from HIV+ patients with oral candidiasis (Zakikhany et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zakikhany et al., 2007.

claim: ERG11 was affected in 70% (7/10) of the patient series with persistent SNPs in four series and mutations in the LOH events in three series.
source: ERG11, which encodes the drug target of fluconazole, was affected in 70% (7/10) of the patient series with persistent SNPs in four series (Patients 9, 14, 30, and 59) and mutations in the LOH events in three series (Patients 1, 15, and 43) (Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5—source data 1A.

claim: HYR3 was persistently mutated in nine of the patients, three of which occurred in LOH tracts.
source: Likewise HYR3, a known virulence gene, was persistently mutated in nine of the patients, three of which occurred in LOH tracts, including one in which a new allele was homozygosed (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1A,B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—source data 1A,B,C.

claim: 171 of the 240 genes were also mutated in an LOH tract in at least one additional patient.
source: More generally, 171 of the 240 genes were also mutated in an LOH tract in at least one additional patient (15/171 in three or more additional patients and 34/171 in two additional patients).
evidence: This is supported by data analysis.

claim: The 240 recurrently mutated genes were partitioned into 5 'co-occurrence clusters' based on the correlation in their mutation occurrence patterns.
source: Next, we partitioned the 240 recurrently mutated genes into 5 'co-occurrence clusters' based on the correlation in their mutation occurrence patterns (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 and Figure 5—source data 1A.

claim: The correlations in co-occurrence clusters are significantly higher than expected in a null model (p < 5.2 × 10−182).
source: These correlations are significantly higher than expected in a null model (p < 5.2 × 10−182, permutation test, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis using a permutation test.

claim: Cluster 1 is enriched for cell wall and cell surface genes.
source: The characterized genes in most of the clusters have coherent functions. Cluster 1 is enriched for cell wall and cell surface genes, Cluster 2 for cell cycle and stress genes, Cluster 3 for genes involved in drug response, and Cluster 5 for carbohydrate binding (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cluster 2 is enriched for cell cycle and stress genes.
source: The characterized genes in most of the clusters have coherent functions. Cluster 1 is enriched for cell wall and cell surface genes, Cluster 2 for cell cycle and stress genes, Cluster 3 for genes involved in drug response, and Cluster 5 for carbohydrate binding (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cluster 3 is enriched for genes involved in drug response.
source: The characterized genes in most of the clusters have coherent functions. Cluster 1 is enriched for cell wall and cell surface genes, Cluster 2 for cell cycle and stress genes, Cluster 3 for genes involved in drug response, and Cluster 5 for carbohydrate binding (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cluster 5 is enriched for carbohydrate binding genes.
source: The characterized genes in most of the clusters have coherent functions. Cluster 1 is enriched for cell wall and cell surface genes, Cluster 2 for cell cycle and stress genes, Cluster 3 for genes involved in drug response, and Cluster 5 for carbohydrate binding (Figure 5, Figure 5—source data 1A).
evidence: This is based on gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Adhesion, filamentation, and virulence in a C. elegans model of infection were measured for a large panel of isolates.
source: Adhesion, filamentation, and virulence in a C. elegans model of infection (Jain et al., 2013) were measured for a large panel of isolates (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6 and citation to Jain et al., 2013.

claim: Competitive fitness in standard tissue culture medium (RPMI) with and without drug was measured in vitro.
source: Additionally, we measured competitive fitness in standard tissue culture medium (RPMI) with and without drug in vitro (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Substantial variation in virulence phenotypes was found between isolates in the same series.
source: We found substantial variation in many of these phenotypes between isolates in the same series (Figure 6 and Figure 7), supporting the notion that the isolates are samples from a broad range of genetic variants within clonal (single infection) populations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Increased fitness in vitro (in the absence of drug) generally correlated with an increase in traits associated with virulence (adhesion, filamentation, and virulence in nematode).
source: In general, increased fitness in vitro (in the absence of drug) correlated with an increase in traits associated with virulence (adhesion, filamentation, and virulence in nematode).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: The later isolates in the series from patients 30 and 43 had increased fitness and higher virulence by all three measures.
source: For example, the later isolates in the series from patients 30 and 43 had increased fitness and higher virulence by all three measures (Figure 6A,B, Figure 7)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6A,B and 7.

claim: A decrease in fitness in isolate 13 of patient 1 was accompanied by a decrease in virulence.
source: whereas, a decrease in fitness in isolate 13 of patient 1 was accompanied by a decrease in virulence (Figures 6C and Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6C and 7.

claim: In patient 59, fitness in vitro decreased while virulence phenotypes increased in a later isolate.
source: A notable exception was patient 59, where fitness in vitro decreased while virulence phenotypes increased in a later isolate (Figures 6D and Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 6D and 7.

claim: In vitro fitness is not always a reflection of virulence.
source: This is consistent with the observations of Noble and co-workers that in vitro fitness is not always a reflection of virulence (Noble et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noble et al., 2010.

claim: When MIC increases first appeared, they were usually accompanied by a decrease in fitness in the absence of drug.
source: When MIC increases first appeared, they were usually accompanied by a decrease in fitness in the absence of drug (Patient 1, isolates 2, 13, and 16, Patients 9, 14, 15 16, and 59, Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A.

claim: Isolates with elevated MIC exhibited increased relative fitness in the presence of the drug.
source: Consistent with the elevated MIC, these isolates exhibited increased relative fitness in the presence of the drug (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7B.

claim: Resistance conferred in C. albicans by gain-of-function mutations in the transcription factors Mrr1, Tac1, and Upc2 is associated with reduced fitness under non-selective conditions in vitro as well as in vivo during colonization of a mammalian host.
source: This is also consistent with a recent study (Sasse et al., 2012) showing that resistance conferred in C. albicans by gain-of-function mutations in the transcription factors Mrr1, Tac1, and Upc2 is associated with reduced fitness under non-selective conditions in vitro as well as in vivo during colonization of a mammalian host.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sasse et al., 2012.

claim: Isolates from later time points were often more fit than those from earlier time points (measured in vitro, in the absence of drug) without further changes in MIC.
source: Consistent with subsequent selection of strains with compensatory variations, isolates from later time points were often more fit than those from earlier time points (measured in vitro, in the absence of drug) without further changes in MIC (e.g., patient 1, isolates 5-7, isolate 14, Figure 7A), with notable exceptions (e.g., isolates 8 and 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7A.

claim: The general trend of fitness recovery is consistent with previous studies in bacteria showing that compensatory mutations may arise to offset the major fitness cost of mutations conferring drug resistance.
source: This general trend is consistent with previous studies in bacteria (Bjorkman and Andersson, 2000); (Gagneux et al., 2006) and in a single documented case in C. glabrata (Singh-Babak et al., 2012), suggesting that compensatory mutations may subsequently arise to offset the major fitness cost of mutations conferring drug resistance.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bjorkman and Andersson, 2000; Gagneux et al., 2006; and Singh-Babak et al., 2012.

claim: Aneuploidies, while largely transient, may be an important intermediate giving rise to more stable adaptive genotypes in some cases.
source: In this context, it appears that aneuploidies (Figure 7A, green), while largely transient, may be an important intermediate giving rise to more stable adaptive genotypes in some cases, as was recently demonstrated in budding yeast adapting to a stressful environment in vitro (Yona et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7A and citation to Yona et al., 2012.

claim: In Patient 1 isolate 13, an increase in MIC and a trisomy of 5 of 8 chromosomes accompanies a large decrease in fitness (in the absence of drug) relative to the preceding isolate 12.
source: For example, in Patient 1 isolate 13, an increase in MIC and a trisomy of 5 of 8 chromosomes accompanies a large decrease in fitness (in the absence of drug) relative to the preceding isolate 12 (Figure 7A) but has increased fitness in the presence of drug (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Patient 1 isolate 13 has increased fitness in the presence of drug.
source: For example, in Patient 1 isolate 13, an increase in MIC and a trisomy of 5 of 8 chromosomes accompanies a large decrease in fitness (in the absence of drug) relative to the preceding isolate 12 (Figure 7A) but has increased fitness in the presence of drug (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7B.

claim: Patient 1 isolate 14 has a similar MIC phenotype to isolate 13 but is euploid and is much more fit.
source: Isolate 14 has a similar MIC phenotype to isolate 13 but is euploid (Figure 3) and is much more fit (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3 and 7A.

claim: Aneuploidy has a general negative effect on fitness.
source: Consistent with the general negative effect of aneuploidy on fitness (Tang and Amon, 2013), the absence of the extra chromosomes resulted in improved overall fitness.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang and Amon, 2013.

claim: 23 recurrently mutated loci had homozygous deletion mutants available from a deletion strain collection.
source: To test the contribution of some of the recurrently identified genes to specific C. albicans phenotypes, we profiled all 23 recurrently mutated loci for which a homozygous deletion mutant was available from a deletion strain collection (Noble et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noble et al., 2010.

claim: Deletion of orf19.4658 caused a twofold decrease in MIC.
source: Deletion of one gene (orf19.4658) caused a twofold decrease in MIC, whereas the other 22 mutants tested did have no significant effect on MIC (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental data from deletion mutant analysis.

claim: 5 of the 22 deletion mutants reduced in vitro fitness in a culture medium thought to approximate in vivo conditions.
source: Consistent with a role in host adaptation, 5 of the 22 deletion mutants reduced in vitro fitness in a culture medium thought to approximate in vivo conditions (Figure 8, 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Three deletion mutants (CCN1, orf19.4471, and one other) were significantly more fit than the WT parental strain.
source: Three were significantly more fit than the WT parental strain (SN250, red, Figure 8), including CCN1, that encodes a G1 cyclin required for hyphal growth maintenance (Loeb et al., 1999) and orf19.4471, an ortholog of Saccharomyces cerevisiae VPS64, which is required for cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting of proteins (Bonangelino et al., 2002), is involved in recycling pheromone receptors (Kemp and Sprague, 2003), and is identified as an 'aneuploidy-tolerating mutant' (Torres et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 and citations to Loeb et al., 1999; Bonangelino et al., 2002; Kemp and Sprague, 2003; Torres et al., 2010.

claim: CCN1 encodes a G1 cyclin required for hyphal growth maintenance.
source: Three were significantly more fit than the WT parental strain (SN250, red, Figure 8), including CCN1, that encodes a G1 cyclin required for hyphal growth maintenance (Loeb et al., 1999) and orf19.4471, an ortholog of Saccharomyces cerevisiae VPS64, which is required for cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting of proteins (Bonangelino et al., 2002), is involved in recycling pheromone receptors (Kemp and Sprague, 2003), and is identified as an 'aneuploidy-tolerating mutant' (Torres et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Loeb et al., 1999.

claim: orf19.4471 is an ortholog of Saccharomyces cerevisiae VPS64, which is required for cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting of proteins.
source: Three were significantly more fit than the WT parental strain (SN250, red, Figure 8), including CCN1, that encodes a G1 cyclin required for hyphal growth maintenance (Loeb et al., 1999) and orf19.4471, an ortholog of Saccharomyces cerevisiae VPS64, which is required for cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting of proteins (Bonangelino et al., 2002), is involved in recycling pheromone receptors (Kemp and Sprague, 2003), and is identified as an 'aneuploidy-tolerating mutant' (Torres et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bonangelino et al., 2002.

claim: orf19.4471 is involved in recycling pheromone receptors.
source: Three were significantly more fit than the WT parental strain (SN250, red, Figure 8), including CCN1, that encodes a G1 cyclin required for hyphal growth maintenance (Loeb et al., 1999) and orf19.4471, an ortholog of Saccharomyces cerevisiae VPS64, which is required for cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting of proteins (Bonangelino et al., 2002), is involved in recycling pheromone receptors (Kemp and Sprague, 2003), and is identified as an 'aneuploidy-tolerating mutant' (Torres et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kemp and Sprague, 2003.

claim: orf19.4471 is identified as an 'aneuploidy-tolerating mutant'.
source: Three were significantly more fit than the WT parental strain (SN250, red, Figure 8), including CCN1, that encodes a G1 cyclin required for hyphal growth maintenance (Loeb et al., 1999) and orf19.4471, an ortholog of Saccharomyces cerevisiae VPS64, which is required for cytoplasm-to-vacuole targeting of proteins (Bonangelino et al., 2002), is involved in recycling pheromone receptors (Kemp and Sprague, 2003), and is identified as an 'aneuploidy-tolerating mutant' (Torres et al., 2010).

claim: Among the least fit deletion mutants were cell wall protein genes (HYR1, HYR3, and PIR1).
source: Among the least fit were cell wall protein genes (HYR1, HYR3, and PIR1; De Groot et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 and citation to De Groot et al., 2003.

claim: The study detected substantial genetic diversity in each series, in contrast to a report of only 26 SNPs detected in a single clinical series of Candida glabrata isolates that spanned a 10-month period.
source: Our study identified substantial genetic diversity in each series, in contrast to the report of only 26 SNPs detected in a single clinical series of Candida glabrata isolates that spanned a 10-month period (Singh-Babak et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from Singh-Babak et al., 2012.

claim: Fluconazole is fungistatic, such that many cells exposed to the drug arrest their growth but do not die.
source: First, fluconazole, the antifungal drug used to treat the patients in our series, is fungistatic, such that many cells exposed to the drug arrest their growth but do not die.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fluconazole's mechanism of action.

claim: The range of diversity in the initial population is not entirely lost when cells are exposed to fungistatic drugs.
source: Thus, the range of diversity in the initial population is not entirely lost.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fungistatic nature of fluconazole.

claim: Caspofungin is an echinocandin fungicidal drug.
source: In contrast, the C. glabrata study involved exposure to caspofungin, an echinocandin fungicidal drug.
evidence: This is established knowledge about caspofungin.

claim: C. albicans is a highly heterozygous diploid whereas C. glabrata is haploid.
source: Second, C. albicans is a highly heterozygous diploid whereas C. glabrata is haploid.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the ploidy of these species.

claim: Mutations can be more readily assimilated in a diploid than in a haploid organism, since deleterious mutations are potentially buffered by a functional version.
source: Mutations can be more readily assimilated in a diploid than in a haploid organism, since deleterious mutations are potentially buffered by a functional version (Thompson et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Thompson et al., 2006.

claim: C. albicans genomes are initially much more diverse (with tens of thousands of heterozygous SNPs in a given isolate).
source: Furthermore, because C. albicans genomes are initially much more diverse (with tens of thousands of heterozygous SNPs in a given isolate), LOH is a high frequency mechanism available to reveal mutations more readily.
evidence: This is based on genomic data from C. albicans.

claim: C. albicans lab isolates likely undergo a stress-induced elevation of mutation and mitotic recombination rates.
source: Third, C. albicans lab isolates likely undergo a stress-induced elevation of mutation and mitotic recombination rates (Ponder et al., 2005; Forche et al., 2011; Rosenberg, 2011), and exposure to a mammalian host results in elevated frequencies of LOH and aneuploidy (Forche et al. 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ponder et al., 2005; Forche et al., 2011; Rosenberg, 2011.

claim: Exposure to a mammalian host results in elevated frequencies of LOH and aneuploidy in C. albicans.
source: Third, C. albicans lab isolates likely undergo a stress-induced elevation of mutation and mitotic recombination rates (Ponder et al., 2005; Forche et al., 2011; Rosenberg, 2011), and exposure to a mammalian host results in elevated frequencies of LOH and aneuploidy (Forche et al. 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Forche et al. 2009.

claim: C. albicans like S. cerevisiae generates large scale genetic variation as a means of adaptation.
source: Thus, C. albicans like S. cerevisiae (Gresham et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Yona et al., 2012; Chang et al., 2013) generates large scale genetic variation as a means of adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gresham et al., 2008; Pavelka et al., 2010; Yona et al., 2012; Chang et al., 2013.

claim: C. albicans is able to tolerate genome and protein diversity.
source: This adds another level of variation to the genome and protein diversity (Santos et al., 2004; Selmecki et al., 2010) that C. albicans is able to tolerate.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Santos et al., 2004 and Selmecki et al., 2010.

claim: LOH in ERG11 has been reported previously.
source: LOH in several genes important for fluconazole resistance has been reported previously for ERG11 (Oliver et al., 2007), TAC1 (Coste et al., 2006), and MRR1 (Schubert et al., 2011), but the degree to which LOH is important in clinical infections was not known.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Oliver et al., 2007.

claim: LOH in TAC1 has been reported previously.
source: LOH in several genes important for fluconazole resistance has been reported previously for ERG11 (Oliver et al., 2007), TAC1 (Coste et al., 2006), and MRR1 (Schubert et al., 2011), but the degree to which LOH is important in clinical infections was not known.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coste et al., 2006.

claim: LOH in MRR1 has been reported previously.
source: LOH in several genes important for fluconazole resistance has been reported previously for ERG11 (Oliver et al., 2007), TAC1 (Coste et al., 2006), and MRR1 (Schubert et al., 2011), but the degree to which LOH is important in clinical infections was not known.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schubert et al., 2011.

claim: In the ten patients studied, LOH was commonly observed and was associated with changes in MIC.
source: In the ten patients studied here, LOH was commonly observed and was associated with changes in MIC.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the study.

claim: LOH of mutations in ERG11 was detected in three patients.
source: As we detected LOH of mutations in ERG11 in three patients, it would be of interest to know if the LOH in these known genes was sufficient to increase MIC, or if other genes within the homozygous region make important contributions.
evidence: This is based on data from the study.

claim: Aneuploidies appeared frequently within the drug-resistant isolates, consistent with previous reports.
source: Aneuploidies appeared frequently within the drug-resistant isolates, consistent with previous reports (Selmecki et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data from the study and citation to Selmecki et al., 2006.

claim: A transient role for aneuploidy is consistent with recent findings from in vitro evolution studies in S. cerevisiae in which a transient aneuploidy was responsible for fitness at elevated temperature, but was eventually replaced by a more stable mutation.
source: A transient role for aneuploidy is consistent with recent findings from in vitro evolution studies in S. cerevisiae (Yona et al., 2012) in which a transient aneuploidy was responsible for fitness at elevated temperature, but was eventually replaced by a more stable mutation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yona et al., 2012.

claim: Variation in intragenic repeat number modulates phenotypic diversity in adhesion and biofilm formation.
source: Variation in intragenic repeat number modulates phenotypic diversity in adhesion and biofilm formation (Verstrepen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Verstrepen et al., 2005.

claim: The functional diversity of cell surface antigens has been proposed to allow rapid adaptation to the environment as well as evasion of the host immune system in fungi and other pathogens.

claim: The evolution of drug resistance in C. albicans has many parallels with the somatic evolution of cancer cells undergoing chemotherapy or treated with specific inhibitors.
source: The evolution of drug resistance in C. albicans has many parallels with the somatic evolution of cancer cells undergoing chemotherapy or treated with specific inhibitors.

claim: Several recent studies have shown a similar spectrum of genetic alterations during the somatic evolution of cancers in patients undergoing chemotherapy or treated with specific inhibitors to those observed in C. albicans.
source: Indeed, several recent studies have shown a similar spectrum of genetic alterations to those observed here during the somatic evolution of cancers in patients undergoing chemotherapy (Podlaha et al., 2012; Landau et al., 2013) or treated with specific inhibitors (Ding et al., 2012) to those observed here.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Podlaha et al., 2012; Landau et al., 2013; and Ding et al., 2012.
